newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Branson starts epic world balloon trip. [CORRECTED 18:41 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Branson starts epic world balloon trip. [CORRECTED 18:41 GMT]

text.p: British tycoon Richard Branson and two co-pilots soared slowly skyward on Tuesday in a giant balloon on a "great adventure", hoping to be the first balloonists to fly round the world.

Watched by his wife Joan and children Holly, 15, and Sam, 11, Branson, and co-pilots Per Lindstrand, 48, and Alex Ritchie, 50, lifted off at 11.19 a.m. (1119 GMT) from an airbase near the ancient Moroccan city of Marrakesh.
"We are now going on a great adventure. I am confident," Branson told reporters, before embracing his family and climbing into the capsule beneath the round balloon, nearly 12-storeys high.
Branson, clad in a green pilot's suit, waved excitedly as the 1.1 million cubic feet (30,000 cubic metres) balloon, filled with hot air and helium, rose against the snow-capped Atlas Mountains.

Per Lindstrand told reporters before entering the capsule, which is fitted with two beds, half a tonne of food, microwave, and complex communications equipment: "I feel fine for the trip. Branson is getting excited."
He said the balloon, Virgin Global Challenger, would travel at 30 to 40 km per hour (19 to 25 mph) over the Atlas and they expected to cross the Algerian border in about 12 hours.
"When we reach the jet stream our speed will accelerate," he said.

Flying eastward, the Branson team will head at around 30,000 ft (10,000 metres) across North Africa, Saudi Arabia and India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and the United States, to land in Britain.
Branson expects the trip to take between 14 and 21 days. "I am enjoying the best experience of my life. I am confident, I am optimistic," he said.
Branson, the flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies, has launched an airline and products ranging from condoms to cola and pensions.
His planned dawn takeoff was delayed by the complexities of inflating the giant balloon, a task taking over 12 hours.
Lift-off was watched by some 300 Moroccan soldiers who had helped British technicians handling the balloon, and by dancers and horsemen who had earlier put on a show to mark the event.

Branson and co-pilot Lindstrand twice came close to death on previous record-breaking balloon flights. This time they are not only battling the elements but racing against American balloonist Steve Fosset who is planning a similar round-the-world attempt, launched from St. Louis, Missouri in the United States.
"I am aware of the competition but I can assure you that we will be one or two days ahead of Steve Fosset," Branson said.
He had to cancel a previous attempt to circumnavigate the globe from Marrakesh last January because of bad weather. He has already crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
According to the Guinness Book of Records the furthest flown by a manned balloon is 8,382 km (5,208 miles), set by American Ben Abruzzo and three co-pilots in 1981 from Japan to California.
Rory McCarthy, one of the original co-pilots on Branson's current flight, was grounded by pneumonia and replaced by Ritchie.
A disappointed, sick McCarthy told reporters just before the balloon took off: "There will be no flight like this one in future. I wish them a good flight."
